title: Time & Work
summary: Rates, LCM units and the men-days chain solve nearly every question: combined work, efficiency ratios, pipes and cisterns, mid-work join/leave, alternate days, provisions and wages. One slot is near-guaranteed in Tier 1, with staged pipe problems and wage splits rising in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Work Rates & the LCM Method
subtopics.concept:
Treat one whole job as the unit of work. A worker who finishes it in T days has a rate of $\dfrac{1}{T}$ per day, and rates add when people work together.

The LCM method keeps everything in whole numbers: set the job to the LCM of the given days, so each rate becomes small units per day.

Two workers who take $a$ and $b$ days alone finish together in $\dfrac{ab}{a+b}$ days.

subtopics.notes:
### What rate means
A job is one whole thing — a wall, a tank, a batch of shirts. A worker's **rate** is the share of that job he finishes in one day.

If A finishes the whole job in T days, his rate is $\dfrac{1}{T}$ per day. Two facts run the whole topic:

$$\text{work} = \text{rate} \times \text{days}, \qquad \text{rates add when people work together}$$

Each worker keeps his own rate inside a team. So the combined time is always less than the fastest single time.

> **Rule:** If your combined answer came out larger than the fastest time, you added days instead of rates.

### The LCM method
Fractions invite slips. Give the job a size in units instead — the LCM of the given days.

A finishes in 15 days, B in 10. Job = 30 units. A does $30 \div 15 = 2$ units a day, B does 3. Together 5 units a day → $30 \div 5 = 6$ days. Every number stays a small whole number to the end.

> **Tip:** Convert every question here to units first. Rates, sums and remainders then stay integers.

### Two workers
For exactly two workers with times a and b:

$$T = \frac{ab}{a+b}$$

6 and 12 days → $\dfrac{72}{18} = 4$ days. This is the LCM method compressed into one line — use it when the numbers divide cleanly.

The reverse is just as common. A and B together take 6 days; A alone takes 15. Subtract rates, never days: $\dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{10}$ → B alone takes 10 days.

### Three or more workers
Add all the rates in units. A, B and C take 9, 12 and 18 days: job = 36 units, rates $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ a day → 4 days. As one formula:

$$T = \frac{abc}{ab + bc + ca}$$

> **Watch:** Do not fold three workers two at a time with $\dfrac{ab}{a+b}$. Add all three rates in a single line.

### Pairwise data
Sometimes the question gives A+B, B+C and A+C instead of single times. Add the three pair-rates: each person appears exactly twice, so halve the sum for the trio rate.

Pairs of 10, 12 and 15 days → $\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ → trio rate $\dfrac{1}{8}$ → 8 days together. For one person alone, subtract the pair that excludes him: A $= \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{24}$ → 24 days.

### Partial work statements
'A can do $\dfrac{5}{6}$ of the work in 10 days.' Scale to the whole job first: full time $= 10 \times \dfrac{6}{5} = 12$ days. Then combine as usual.

In units it is equally direct: a 24-unit job with 20 units done in 10 days gives a rate of $\dfrac{20}{10} = 2$ units a day. Small numbers, same answer.

> **Careful:** Multiply the days by the reciprocal of the fraction, not by the fraction itself.

### Fraction of work left
A team that takes T days together finishes $\dfrac{t}{T}$ of the job in t days, leaving $1 - \dfrac{t}{T}$.

A and B together take 12 days. After 5 days together, $\dfrac{5}{12}$ is done and $\dfrac{7}{12}$ is left. That remainder then belongs to whoever keeps working — usually the first step of a longer question.

> **Note:** The leftover fraction is itself a common exam answer. Compute it exactly; do not round it.

patterns.name: Fractional / partial work statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'A can do 3/5 of the work in 12 days', 'B does 2/7 of the work in 8 days' — the full-work time, or the together time, is asked.
steps: Scale each statement to the whole job: days × reciprocal of the fraction.
Combine the full-work times like any other question.

example.q: A can do $\dfrac{5}{6}$ of a work in 10 days and B can do $\dfrac{3}{8}$ of the same work in 9 days. Working together, in how many days will they complete the work?

patterns.name: Fraction of work left after t days together
patterns.howToSpot: A team's together time and the days they worked are given; the fraction of work left — or who finishes the rest — is asked.
steps: Read off the together time T of the team as it stood.
Left $= 1 - \dfrac{t}{T}$; if a new worker finishes the rest, multiply the leftover by his full time.
patterns.why: A team working at its combined rate covers the whole job in T days, so t days deliver exactly t/T of it.

example.q: A and B together can finish a work in 12 days. They work together for 5 days, after which B leaves. In how many days will C alone finish the remaining work if C alone can do the whole work in 24 days?

revision: Rate = 1/time; rates add; work = rate × days.
Two workers: T = ab/(a+b). Three: T = abc/(ab+bc+ca).
Together minus one: subtract rates, never days.
Pairwise times: add the three pair-rates, halve for the trio.
Partial work: full time = days × reciprocal of the fraction.
Work left after t days together: 1 − t/T.

subtopics.title: Efficiency, 'Twice as Good' & Ratio Cases
subtopics.concept:
Efficiency is rate: the share of a job a person finishes per day. Efficiency and time are inversely proportional — twice as efficient means half the days.

If A is k times as efficient as B and together they take T days, the job is $(k+1)T$ units: B alone needs $(k+1)T$ days and A alone $\dfrac{(k+1)T}{k}$ days.

Convert every 'twice as good' or '50% more efficient' statement into a rate ratio before doing anything else.

subtopics.notes:
### Efficiency is rate
'Efficient' here simply means faster. Efficiency is another word for rate, and it moves opposite to time:

$$\frac{\text{efficiency of A}}{\text{efficiency of B}} = \frac{\text{days of B}}{\text{days of A}}$$

Twice as efficient means half the days. Three times as efficient means one-third of the days. Write every comparison as a rate ratio before touching the numbers.

> **Rule:** Rate × days = one whole job. Multiply the rate by k and the days must divide by k.

### The unit trick
A is k times as good as B. Let B do 1 unit a day and A do k units a day — together $(k+1)$ units a day. If they finish in T days, the whole job is $(k+1)T$ units:

- weaker worker alone: $(k+1)T$ days
- stronger worker alone: $\dfrac{(k+1)T}{k}$ days

A is twice as good as B, and together they take 18 days → job $= 3 \times 18 = 54$ units → B alone 54 days, A alone 27. The weaker worker takes the longer time, always.

> **Watch:** If the stronger worker got the bigger number of days, the ratio was inverted.

### Ratios and per cents
'A and B are in efficiency ratio 3 : 2' is the same idea with both rates written at once: rates $3u$ and $2u$, together $5u$. If B alone takes 30 days, $2u = \dfrac{1}{30}$, so $u = \dfrac{1}{60}$ and together $5u = \dfrac{1}{12}$ → 12 days.

Per cents become ratios at sight. 50% more efficient → 3 : 2. 25% more → 5 : 4. 20% less → 4 : 5. Then continue exactly as with a plain ratio.

> **Tip:** '25% more efficient' is 125 : 100 = 5 : 4, never 25 : 100.

### Days-difference questions
'A is twice as fast as B and takes 12 days less.' Efficiency ratio 2 : 1 makes the times 1x and 2x. The gap $2x - x = 12$ gives x = 12: A takes 12 days, B takes 24. Together they need $\dfrac{12 \times 24}{36} = 8$ days.

In general, with efficiency ratio a : b, the times run b : a. Call them bx and ax, put the difference equal to the given gap, and solve for x.

### Difference of their times
Exams often ask for the difference of the two times instead of one of them. Price the job first, then subtract.

A is 3 times as efficient as B, and together they take 12 days → job $= 4 \times 12 = 48$ units. B alone 48 days, A alone 16 days, difference 32 days. One subtraction after the pricing step.

### Keep the direction honest
The strongest worker always takes the fewest days — and later, in wage questions, earns the bigger share. Run that check on every answer before choosing the option.

Recompute one full chain to stay safe: A is twice as good as B, together 9 days → job = 27 units → B alone 27 days, A alone 13.5. The weaker worker's days equal the job size in units — no accident, since the weaker worker sets the unit at 1 a day.

> **Note:** '30% more efficient' means 13 : 10, not 30 : 100. Convert the wording to a ratio before any arithmetic.

subtopics.title: Pipes & Cisterns
subtopics.concept:
A tank is filled by some pipes and emptied by others. A pipe that **fills** is an *inlet*. A pipe or a leak that **empties** is an *outlet*.

Treat it exactly like a time-and-work question. Inlets do positive work, outlets do negative work. The quickest method: take the tank's capacity as the **LCM of all the times**, so every pipe's speed becomes a whole number of units per hour.

mistakes.wrong: Adding the emptying pipe's speed as if it fills the tank.
mistakes.right: Put a minus sign in front of every outlet or leak before adding.

mistakes.wrong: Using $\dfrac{ab}{a+b}$ for one filling and one emptying pipe.
mistakes.right: That formula is for two inlets. For fill + empty use $\dfrac{ab}{b-a}$.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the stage-2 time when the question asks for the total time.
mistakes.right: Underline the last line: extra time or total time. Add the stages if it says total.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the tank is already part-full when a new pipe is opened.
mistakes.right: Find the water still needed first, then divide by the new speed.

mistakes.wrong: In alternate-pipe questions, counting full rounds past the point where the tank is full.
mistakes.right: Before each hour, check whether the water left is less than that pipe fills in an hour.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing minutes and hours (8 h 40 min taken as 8.4 hours).
mistakes.right: Convert first: 40 minutes = $\dfrac{2}{3}$ hour, so 8 h 40 min = $\dfrac{26}{3}$ hours.

subtopics.notes:
### The basic idea
Every question gives you pipes and the time each one takes on its own.

- An **inlet** fills the tank. Count its work as **plus (+)**.
- An **outlet** or a **leak** empties the tank. Count its work as **minus (−)**.
- "A fills the tank in 6 hours" means A fills $\frac{1}{6}$ of the tank every hour.

> **Rule:** Fill = plus, empty = minus. Write the sign next to every pipe before you calculate anything.

### The LCM method (use it every time)
Fractions like $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{18}$ are slow and easy to get wrong. Give the tank a number of units instead.

1. Tank capacity = LCM of all the given times.
2. Speed of each pipe = capacity ÷ its time (units per hour).
3. Net speed = inlets added, outlets subtracted.
4. Time = capacity ÷ net speed.

> **Example:** A fills a tank in 12 hours, B in 18 hours. Tank = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units. A fills 3 units/hour, B fills 2 units/hour. Together: 5 units/hour, so $36 \div 5 = 7.2$ hours = **7 hours 12 minutes**.

### When one pipe empties the tank
Use the same method. Just subtract the emptying pipe.

A fills in 6 hours, B empties in 9 hours. Tank = 18 units. A = +3, B = −2, so net = +1 unit/hour. The tank fills in **18 hours**.

For exactly one filling pipe (a hours) and one emptying pipe (b hours):
$$T = \frac{a \times b}{b - a}$$
Check: $\frac{6 \times 9}{9 - 6} = 18$ hours.

> **Watch:** If the emptying pipe is faster, the net speed is negative. A full tank will empty; an empty tank will never fill.

### Pipes opened or closed in between
Split the question into stages. The tank only cares how much water is already in it.

1. Stage 1: water filled = speed × time.
2. Water still needed = capacity − water filled.
3. Stage 2: water still needed ÷ new net speed.

A (10 h) and B (15 h) run for 2 hours. Tank = 30 units, speed 5, so 10 units are filled and 20 are left. Now a drain C (30 h) opens: net speed = 5 − 1 = 4. The rest takes 5 hours, so the total is **7 hours**.

> **Watch:** Read the last line carefully. Some questions ask for the *extra* time (5 hours), others for the *total* time (7 hours).

### Finding the leak
"A tank normally fills in 8 hours. Because of a leak, it now takes 10 hours. How long will the leak take to empty the full tank?"

Tank = LCM(8, 10) = 40 units. Normal speed = 5, speed with the leak = 4. The difference, 1 unit/hour, is the leak. So the leak empties the tank in **40 hours**.

> **Tip:** Leak time = $\frac{t_1 \times t_2}{t_2 - t_1}$ where $t_1$ is the normal time and $t_2$ the slower time: $\frac{8 \times 10}{2} = 40$.

### Pipes opened one after the other
Some questions open the pipes turn by turn, one hour each. Treat one full round as a single unit of time.

A fills in 4 hours, B in 6 hours. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A. Tank = 12 units, A = 3, B = 2, so one round (2 hours) fills 5 units. After 2 rounds (4 hours) 10 units are filled and 2 are left. It is A's turn: 2 units at 3 per hour take $\frac{2}{3}$ hour = 40 minutes. Total = **4 hours 40 minutes**.

> **Watch:** Before counting the last round, check whether the tank gets full *during* the round. Stop there.

### When the answer is in litres
If one pipe's speed is given in litres, the capacity is a real number. Write every pipe's speed in litres per hour and solve for the capacity.

A leak empties a full tank in 6 hours. An inlet that fills 4 litres a minute (240 litres an hour) is opened, and now the full tank empties in 8 hours. Leak − inlet = capacity ÷ 8:
$$\frac{C}{6} - 240 = \frac{C}{8} \Rightarrow \frac{C}{24} = 240 \Rightarrow C = 5760 \text{ litres}$$

steps: Normal speed = 4, speed with the leak = 3.

patterns.name: A pipe is opened or closed in between
patterns.howToSpot: Pipes run for some time, then a pipe is added or removed. The remaining time or the total time is asked.
steps: Water still needed = tank − water filled.
Stage 2: divide what is left by the new net speed.
Add the stages if the total time is asked.
patterns.why: The tank does not care how the water got there. Each stage is a fresh, smaller question.

example.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 hours and 16 hours. Both are opened for 4 hours. Then a drain that can empty the full tank in 24 hours is also opened. In how many more hours will the tank be full?
steps: Tank = LCM(12, 16, 24) = 48 units. A = 4, B = 3, drain = −2.
First 4 hours: $7 \times 4 = 28$ units, so 20 units are left.
New net speed = 7 − 2 = 5 units per hour.

patterns.name: Pipes opened one after the other
patterns.howToSpot: The pipes are opened in turns, one hour (or one minute) each: "alternately" or "A, then B, then A…".
steps: Take tank = LCM of the times.
Water filled in one round = sum of the speeds in that round.
Count the full rounds that fit without filling the tank.
Finish the last part pipe by pipe; stop the moment the tank is full.
patterns.why: The pattern repeats every round, so full rounds can be counted in one step. Only the last round needs care.

example.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 3 hours and pipe B in 4 hours. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A. In how much time will the tank be full?
steps: One round (A then B, 2 hours) = 7 units.
After 1 round: 7 units in 2 hours, 5 left.
A's hour adds 4 (3 hours, 1 left). B needs $\frac{1}{3}$ hour = 20 minutes for the last unit.

patterns.name: Tank capacity in litres
patterns.howToSpot: One pipe's speed is given in litres per minute or per hour, and the tank's capacity is asked.
steps: Change every speed to the same unit (litres per hour).
Write each pipe's speed with C as the capacity, e.g. C/5.
Make an equation from the net speed.
patterns.why: A speed in litres fixes the size of the tank, so the capacity is a real number, not LCM units.

example.q: A leak can empty a full tank in 5 hours. An inlet pipe that fills 3 litres a minute is opened, and now the full tank empties in 20 hours. What is the capacity of the tank?

patterns.name: When was a pipe closed?
patterns.howToSpot: Two pipes start together, one is closed after some time, and the tank still fills in a given total time. The closing time is asked.
steps: Take tank = LCM of the times.
The pipe that was never closed works for the whole time: find its water.
The rest of the water came from the closed pipe.
Its working time = its water ÷ its speed.

subtopics.notes:
### Work is a product
Many men in few days or few men in many days — the job keeps the same size. Total work is the product of every resource:

$$W = M \times D \times H \times E$$

men × days × hours a day × efficiency. For the same job, equate two situations: $M_1 D_1 H_1 E_1 = M_2 D_2 H_2 E_2$. 18 men × 25 days = 450 man-days; with 30 men the same job needs $\dfrac{450}{30} = 15$ days.

> **Rule:** For a fixed job, more men means fewer days. Men and days are inversely proportional.

### Hours join the chain
Hours a day behave exactly like men. 12 men working 8 hours a day for 15 days put in $12 \times 15 \times 8 = 1440$ man-hours. With 18 men at 10 hours a day the job takes $\dfrac{1440}{180} = 8$ days.

Write the missing quantity last, then divide. No proportion table is needed.

> **Tip:** Convert the whole job to one labour unit first — man-days or man-hours. The answer is then a single division.

### Provisions
Food 'for M men for D days' is $M \times D$ man-days of stock. After t days the stock left is $M(D - t)$, and the new headcount consumes it:

$$\text{days left} = \frac{M_1(D - t)}{M_2}$$

400 men hold 25 days of food. After 5 days, 100 more men arrive: $400 \times 20 = 8000$ man-days ÷ 500 men = 16 days. Men leaving works the same way, and then the stock lasts longer.

> **Watch:** Subtract the elapsed days before anything else. Feeding the new headcount from the full D is the standard error.

### Mid-work changes
A team works for a while, then men join or leave. Convert the whole job to man-days, subtract what is already done, and hand the remainder to the new team.

60 men need 40 days → 2400 man-days. After 10 days, 600 are done. Ten men leave, and the remaining 1800 man-days need $\dfrac{1800}{50} = 36$ days more.

> **Careful:** Apply the chain to the remaining work only. Restarting from the full job double-counts the finished part.

### Men, women and boys
'3 men or 5 women can do it in 12 days' fixes both unit rates, because both teams finish equal work. So one man does $\dfrac{1}{36}$ per day and one woman $\dfrac{1}{60}$ per day.

Price any mixed team by adding rates: 6 men + 5 women $= \dfrac{6}{36} + \dfrac{5}{60} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ → 4 days.

> **Tip:** Read 'or' as 'the two teams are equal in work terms'. The two unit rates then fall out together.

### Scaling the work itself
Sometimes the work grows instead of the crew. Work then scales directly with men and days:

$$W_2 = W_1 \times \frac{M_2}{M_1} \times \frac{D_2}{D_1}$$

8 men reap 20 hectares in 12 days. In 9 days, 20 men reap $20 \times \dfrac{20}{8} \times \dfrac{9}{12} = 37.5$ hectares. Multiply for resources that grew, divide for those that shrank.

### Efficiency inside the product
A worker twice as efficient counts as two men. A team of 3 men and 2 boys, where one man equals 2 boys in output, is $3 \times 2 + 2 = 8$ boy-units. Convert everyone to one standard unit before multiplying — never mix raw headcounts with a separate efficiency factor.

subtopics.notes:
### Count the work actually done
Someone leaves, someone joins late, people alternate days, wages get split — one method answers all of it. Put the job in LCM units, write each worker's daily rate, then add up the work each person actually did. Set the total equal to the whole job.

### Leaving after t days
A works t of his $T_A$ days and stops. He finished $\dfrac{t}{T_A}$ of the job; the rest, $1 - \dfrac{t}{T_A}$, belongs to whoever continues.

A (12 days) works 3 days → $\dfrac{1}{4}$ done. B (18 days) alone needs $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 18 = 13.5$ days.

> **Rule:** Work done = rate × days worked. Whoever continues inherits only the remainder.

### Leaving before the end
'A leaves 3 days before the work finishes' hides the total time T. Write both stints against T: A works $T - 3$ days, B works all T days.

$$\frac{T - t}{T_A} + \frac{T}{T_B} = 1$$

With $T_A = 12$, $T_B = 18$, $t = 3$: $\dfrac{T-3}{12} + \dfrac{T}{18} = 1$ → $3(T-3) + 2T = 36$ → T = 9 days.

> **Tip:** One unknown T, one linear equation. Multiply through by the LCM of the two times.

### Joining after t days
A starts alone; B joins later. Add the solo stint to the team stint:

$$\frac{t}{T_A} + (\text{days together}) \times \left(\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}\right) = 1$$

A (20 days) works 5 days → $\dfrac{1}{4}$. The pair then does $\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{7}{60}$ a day → $\dfrac{45}{7} = 6\dfrac{3}{7}$ days more, $11\dfrac{3}{7}$ in total.

> **Watch:** 'In how many days is the work finished?' can mean the total or the extra days after the change. Underline which one is asked.

### Alternate days
Pair the days into one cycle of two days: A's day plus B's day $= \dfrac{1}{T_A} + \dfrac{1}{T_B}$ of the job. Count whole cycles, then walk the leftover day by day — the next day is the other worker's turn.

A = 8 days (3 units of 24), B = 12 days (2 units). A cycle = 5 units. Four cycles = 8 days, 20 units done. Day 9 is A's: 3 more, 1 left. Day 10 is B's at 2 a day: half a day. Total $9\dfrac{1}{2}$ days.

> **Careful:** The tail does not always fit the pattern. Check whose turn the next day really is.

### Wages follow work
Money splits in the ratio of work actually delivered: rate × days for each person. When everyone works the full time, the days cancel and the wage ratio is just the rate ratio.

A alone 10 days, B alone 15, ₹600 earned together → rates 3 : 2 → ₹360 and ₹240. An unknown member: his rate = team rate − the known rates. A (12 days), B (20 days) and C finish in 5 days → C $= \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{15}$; the shares run 5 : 3 : 4.

### Read the question twice
The same numbers support four different asks: total days, days after the change, each person's share of work, each person's share of money. Mark the words *total*, *more*, *alone* and *remaining* before computing. Most lost marks here are reading losses, not arithmetic ones.

example.q: A can finish a job in 15 days and B in 10 days. How long will they take together?
example.solution:
Job = 30 units
A does 30 ÷ 15 = 2 a day, B does 30 ÷ 10 = 3 a day
Together = 5 a day
Time = 30 ÷ 5 = **6 days**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Pipes fill a tank and another pipe empties it. Asks the time to fill.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Filling pipes count as +, emptying pipes as −.
Add them up to get the net work per hour.

example.q: A pipe fills a tank in 12 hours. Another empties the full tank in 24 hours. With both open, how long to fill?
example.solution:
Tank = 24 units
Filling: 24 ÷ 12 = +2 an hour. Emptying: 24 ÷ 24 = −1 an hour
Net = 2 − 1 = 1 an hour
Time = **24 hours**

pyqPatterns.approach:
Give the slower worker 1 unit a day. The faster gets 2 (or 3, ...).
Total job = units a day together × days.

B alone = 54 ÷ 1 = **54 days**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Someone leaves or joins in the middle
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One person works a few days and then leaves (or joins late). Asks the time left.

Work done = work per day × days.
Take it off the job. The rest goes to whoever is left.

example.q: A can do a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works 3 days and leaves. How long does B take to finish?

Job = 36 units. A does 3 a day, B does 2 a day
A in 3 days: 3 × 3 = 9 units
Left: 36 − 9 = 27 units
B finishes in 27 ÷ 2 = **13.5 days**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A and B work one day each, turn by turn. Asks when the job is done.
pyqPatterns.approach:

Count the rounds, then check any leftover day.

example.q: A can do a job in 3 days and B in 6 days. They work on alternate days, A first. When is it done?
example.solution:
Job = 6 units. A does 2 a day, B does 1 a day
One round of 2 days = 2 + 1 = 3 units
6 units needs 2 rounds
2 rounds = **4 days**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The same work is done in two situations with different men, days or hours per day.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the total man-hours for the first case.

example.solution:
Total work = 12 × 8 × 15 = 1440 man-hours

example.solution:
Food left after 5 days = 400 × 20 = 8000 man-days
Men now = 400 + 100 = 500
Days = 8000 ÷ 500 = **16 days**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Some people do a job together and get a total payment. Asks one person's share.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Share the pay in the ratio of work each did.
With equal days, that is the ratio of their daily work.

Job = 30 units. A does 3 a day, B does 2 a day
Ratio A : B = 3 : 2
A's share = 3/5 of 600 = **₹360**

Times: $x$ and $3x$ with $3x - x = 24$ ⇒ $x = 12$ (A = 12, B = 36).
Together: $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9}$ ⇒ 9 days.
practice.shortcut: Difference of times = 2 units = 24 ⇒ A 12, B 36; ab/(a+b) = 9.

practice.q: A can complete a piece of work in 15 days and B can complete it in 10 days. Working together, they will complete it in:
practice.solution: LCM method: job $= 30$ units. A: 2 units/day, B: 3 units/day → 5 units/day → $\frac{30}{5} = 6$ days.

A, B and C can complete a piece of work in 9 days, 12 days and 18 days respectively. Working together, they will complete it in:
practice.solution: Job $= 36$ units (LCM of 9, 12, 18). Rates: $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ units/day → $\frac{36}{9} = 4$ days.

practice.shortcut: All three pair-numbers share LCM 60 — put everything over 60 in one line.

practice.q: A and B together can do a piece of work in 10 days, B and C together in 12 days, and A and C together in 15 days. All three working together will finish it in:
practice.solution:
Sum of pair rates $= \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{6+5+4}{60} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Trio rate $= \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8}$ → 8 days.

practice.q: A and B together take 12 days, B and C together 15 days, and A and C together 20 days for the same work. A alone can do it in:
A can do $\frac{3}{5}$ of a work in 12 days and B can do $\frac{2}{7}$ of the same work in 8 days. Working together, they will complete the work in:
practice.solution:
A's full-work time $= 12 \times \frac{5}{3} = 20$ days; B's $= 8 \times \frac{7}{2} = 28$ days.
Together: $\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{28} = \frac{7+5}{140} = \frac{3}{35}$ → $\frac{35}{3} = 11\frac{2}{3}$ days.

practice.q: A does $\frac{5}{6}$ of a piece of work in 10 days, and B does $\frac{3}{8}$ of the same work in 9 days. Working together, they finish the whole work in:
practice.solution:
A's full-work time $= 10 \times \frac{6}{5} = 12$ days; B's $= 9 \times \frac{8}{3} = 24$ days.
Together: $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{24} = \frac{1}{8}$ → 8 days.
practice.shortcut: Multiply the days by the reciprocal of the fraction — not by the fraction itself.

practice.q: A is twice as efficient as B, and together they complete a work in 18 days. B alone can complete it in:
practice.solution: Job $= (2+1) \times 18 = 54$ units → B alone $= 54$ days. (A alone $= 27$ days.)
practice.shortcut: Weaker worker gets the LONGER time — $(k+1)T$ belongs to B.

practice.q: A is thrice as efficient as B, and together they finish a work in 12 days. A alone will finish it in:
A is 4 times as efficient as B, and working together they complete a job in 10 days. B alone will complete it in:
practice.solution: Job $= 5 \times 10 = 50$ units → B alone 50 days (A alone 12.5 days).

practice.q: The efficiencies of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 2, and together they finish a work in 15 days. B alone will finish it in:
practice.solution: Rates $3u$ and $2u$ → job $= 5u \times 15 = 75u$. B alone $= \frac{75u}{2u} = 37.5$ days.

practice.q: A and B work with efficiencies in the ratio 3 : 2. B alone can complete the work in 30 days. Working together, they will complete it in:
The efficiencies of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 2. B alone takes 40 days for a piece of work. Working together, A and B will take:
A is twice as fast a worker as B and takes 12 days less than B for the same work. Working together, they will finish the work in:
practice.solution:
Times: $x$ and $2x$ with $2x - x = 12$ → A = 12, B = 24.
Together $= \frac{12 \times 24}{12 + 24} = 8$ days.

practice.q: A works 1.5 times as fast as B (efficiencies 3 : 2). Together they finish a job in 20 days. B alone will finish it in:
A is thrice as fast as B, and B takes 36 days more than A to complete a piece of work. Working together, they will complete it in:

A is 25% more efficient than B and therefore takes 12 days less than B for the same work. Working together, they will finish the work in:
practice.solution:
Ratio $5:4$ → times $4x$ and $5x$ with $5x - 4x = 12$ → B = 60, A = 48.
Together: $\frac{48 \times 60}{108} = \frac{80}{3} = 26\frac{2}{3}$ days.

practice.q: Two pipes can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours respectively. If both pipes are opened together, the tank will be filled in:
practice.solution: Tank $= 30$ units. Rates 3 and 2 units/h → $\frac{30}{5} = 6$ hours.

practice.q: Three pipes can fill a tank in 20 hours, 30 hours and 60 hours respectively. Opening all three together, the tank is filled in:
A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours and another pipe can empty the full tank in 24 hours. If both are opened, the empty tank will be filled in:
Two pipes fill a tank in 9 hours and 12 hours, while a third pipe empties it in 18 hours. With all three open, the empty tank is filled in:
Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 8 hours and 12 hours respectively, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 24 hours. All three are opened together. The tank will be full in:
practice.solution: Tank $= 24$ units. Net rate $= 3 + 2 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 6 hours.

practice.q: With a leak at its bottom, a tank takes 20 hours to fill, while without the leak it fills in 12 hours. The leak alone can empty the full tank in:
A cistern is normally filled in 8 hours, but takes 8 hours 40 minutes to fill because of a leak in its bottom. In how many hours will the leak alone empty the full cistern?
practice.solution: Slow time $= 8\frac{2}{3} = \frac{26}{3}$ h. Leak rate $= \frac{1}{8} - \frac{3}{26} = \frac{13-12}{104} = \frac{1}{104}$ → 104 hours.

practice.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 10 hours and 15 hours. Both are opened together for 2 hours; then a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 30 hours, is also opened. The total time taken to fill the tank is:
practice.solution:
Tank = 30 units; stage 1: $5 \times 2 = 10$ units done, 20 left.
Stage 2: net $= 5 - 1 = 4$ units/h → 5 more hours. Total $= 2 + 5 = 7$ hours.

practice.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 20 hours respectively. Both are opened together for 4 hours; then B is closed and a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 30 hours, is opened along with A. The total time taken to fill the tank is:
practice.solution:
Tank = 60 units. Stage 1: $(5+3) \times 4 = 32$ units done, 28 left.
Stage 2: net $= 5 - 2 = 3$ units/h → $\frac{28}{3} = 9\frac{1}{3}$ h more. Total $= 13\frac{1}{3}$ hours.

practice.shortcut: Fewer men → the stock lasts longer than the original 35 remaining days.

practice.q: 60 men can complete a piece of work in 40 days. They start together and work for 10 days, after which 10 men leave. In how many days will the remaining work be finished?
practice.solution: Job $= 2400$ man-days; done $= 600$; left $= 1800$ with 50 men → 36 days.

120 men can complete a piece of work in 60 days. They work together for the first 12 days; after that some men leave, and the remaining men complete the rest of the work in 72 days. How many men left after the 12th day?
practice.solution:
Job $= 7200$ man-days; done $= 1440$; left $= 5760$.
Men needed $= \frac{5760}{72} = 80$ → $120 - 80 = 40$ men must leave.

practice.q: A can do a piece of work in 12 days and B can do it in 18 days. A works for 3 days and then leaves. B alone will finish the remaining work in:
practice.solution: A did $\frac{3}{12} = \frac14$; remaining $= \frac34$. B's time $= \frac34 \times 18 = 13.5$ days.

practice.q: A and B together receive ₹600 for completing a job. A alone can do the job in 10 days and B alone in 15 days. A's share is:
A can complete a work in 20 days and B in 15 days. A works alone for 5 days, after which B joins him. In how many days in total is the work completed?
practice.solution:
A alone did $\frac{5}{20} = \frac14$. Remaining $\frac34$ at $\frac{7}{60}$/day → $\frac{45}{7} = 6\frac37$ days.
Total $= 5 + 6\frac37 = 11\frac37$ days.

practice.q: A can complete a job in 3 days and B in 6 days. They work on alternate days, A starting on day 1. The job is finished in:
practice.solution: Per 2-day cycle: $\frac13 + \frac16 = \frac12$. Two cycles = 4 days complete the job exactly.

practice.q: A can do a work in 10 days, B in 15 days and C in 30 days. All three start together, but A leaves after 2 days. For how many more days will B and C work to finish the job?
practice.solution:
Job = 30 units; rates 3, 2, 1. In 2 days all three did 12 units; 18 left.
B + C = 3 units/day → $18 \div 3 = 6$ days.

practice.q: A can finish a piece of work in 12 days and B in 24 days. A starts the work and B joins him after 6 days. The whole work is finished in:
practice.solution:
A alone: $\frac{6}{12} = \frac12$ done. Remaining $\frac12$ at $\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{24} = \frac18$/day → 4 days.
Total $= 6 + 4 = 10$ days.

practice.q: A, B and C together complete a job for ₹4,500. A alone can do it in 10 days, B in 12 days and C in 15 days. B's share is:
A can finish a work in 8 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. The work is finished in:
practice.solution:
Job 24 units; A 3/day, B 2/day; cycle = 5 units per 2 days.
4 cycles = 8 days → 20 done. Day 9 (A): 3 → 1 left. Day 10 (B, 2/day): $\frac12$ day.
Total $= 9\frac12$ days.
practice.shortcut: Day 9 belongs to A, not B — the turns alternate every single day.
